introduction-why-naming-the-beast-matter.core: Bugs come in different kinds (deterministic, observer-sensitive, emergent, latent, decay). Naming the kind first tells you which debugging strategy will work.

first_principles.problem: Engineers dive into code with a debugger for every bug. That works for some and wastes days on others that vanish when observed or only appear under rare interactions.
truths: Different bug types respond to different techniques.
derivation: Ask first: **does it reproduce reliably?** **Does observing change it?** **Is it emergent?**
Pick tools accordingly: debugger, logging/tracing, chaos testing, dependency pinning.

analogy.title: Diagnosis before surgery
analogy.story: A doctor decides whether it's a broken bone or a virus before treating. Surgery on a virus is useless.
analogy.breaks: Medical categories are well defined. Bug categories overlap, so classification is a starting hypothesis.

example.title: An intermittent checkout failure

steps.label: Choice
steps.detail: Breakpoints would change timing; distributed tracing captures it without pausing.

example.outcome: the right tool is chosen from the start.

check.a: Because the effective debugging technique depends on the bug's nature.

bohrbugs-the-deterministic-failures.core: A Bohrbug fails the same way every time under the same conditions. It's the easiest kind: reproduce, isolate, fix, and add a regression test.

first_principles.problem: A function always returns the wrong total for orders with discounts. It's annoying, but completely predictable.
truths: Tests can pin it down permanently.

analogy.title: A broken light switch
analogy.story: Flip it and the light stays off, every time, for everyone. You know exactly where to look.
analogy.breaks: Switches have one failure mode. Code can have several Bohrbugs masking each other.

example.title: Wrong discount total
example.scenario: Orders with two coupons total incorrectly.

steps.label: Bisect
steps.detail: The failing commit changed coupon stacking order.

code.text: git bisect start && git bisect bad HEAD && git bisect good v2.3.0

example.outcome: fixed once and protected by a test forever.

check.q: What's the best tool to find which commit introduced a Bohrbug?

heisenbugs-the-observer-dependent-failur.core: A Heisenbug disappears or changes when you try to observe it, because debugging alters timing, memory layout or optimisation. Use low-overhead observation instead of pausing the program.

first_principles.problem: A race condition crashes in production but never under the debugger, because breakpoints and logs change the timing that triggers it.
derivation: Use **non-intrusive** tools: tracing, sampling profilers, core dumps.
Increase **concurrency or load** to provoke it.

analogy.title: A car rattle that stops at the mechanic
analogy.story: The noise vanishes when the mechanic listens, and returns on the drive home.
analogy.breaks: Cars rattle for physical reasons. Heisenbugs are often timing races that need special tools.

example.title: Crash under load only
example.scenario: A Go service panics 1 in 10,000 requests.

steps.label: Tool
steps.detail: The race detector reports two goroutines writing a shared map.

example.outcome: the hidden race is found without changing timing by hand.

check.q: Why do breakpoints often hide race conditions?
check.a: They change thread timing, so the problematic interleaving no longer happens.

mandelbugs-the-deeply-complex-failures.core: A Mandelbug arises from so many interacting factors that it looks chaotic, though it's deterministic underneath. Find it by narrowing conditions and correlating many signals, not by stepping through code.

first_principles.problem: A memory spike happens only with a certain traffic mix, a specific GC setting, a cron job and one tenant's large payloads. No single factor explains it.
derivation: **Slice by dimensions** (tenant, version, region) to find what's different.
**Reduce the system**: isolate components until it stops.

analogy.title: A fractal
analogy.story: The closer you zoom, the more detail appears: there's always another layer of cause.
analogy.breaks: Fractals are infinite; real bugs eventually have a finite set of causes you can find.

example.title: Memory spike every few days

steps.label: Observability
steps.detail: Per-request events with tenant and payload size made the pattern visible.

example.outcome: an apparently random bug resolves into a specific combination.

check.q: How is a Mandelbug different from a Heisenbug?
check.a: A Heisenbug hides when observed; a Mandelbug is caused by complex interactions that make it look chaotic.

schroedinbugs-the-bugs-that-shouldnt-hav.core: A Schroedinbug is code that was always wrong but worked by luck, until something (a review, a refactor, new data) exposes it and it starts failing.

first_principles.problem: An off-by-one error ran for two years because the data never hit the edge case. A refactor or new input finally triggers it, and everyone wonders how it ever worked.
derivation: When code 'shouldn't work', **investigate why it did**.
Be careful when **inputs change** (new customers, migrations).

analogy.title: A cracked foundation that held for years
analogy.story: The house stood fine until heavier furniture arrived, then the crack mattered.
analogy.breaks: Cracks are visible on inspection. Latent bugs often need specific inputs to appear.

example.title: Pagination off-by-one
example.scenario: Page size 100 skips one record when totals exceed 10,000.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.detail: Property test: every record appears exactly once across pages.

example.outcome: the latent bug is fixed and its class tested.

check.a: A change in context: new inputs, a refactor, or someone reading the code closely.

software-rot-bit-rot.core: Unchanged code breaks over time because its environment changes: dependencies, APIs, certificates, OS versions, data shapes. Fight rot with pinning, regular updates and continuous testing.

first_principles.problem: A deployment script untouched for three years fails today. The code didn't change; the world around it did.

analogy.title: A car left in a garage
analogy.story: Untouched for years, the tyres deflate, the battery dies and the fuel goes stale, though nobody 'changed' the car.
analogy.breaks: Cars rot physically. Software rots through its environment, so the fix is exercise and updates.

example.title: The 3-year-old deploy script

steps.label: Prevention
steps.detail: A nightly run would have caught it months earlier.

example.outcome: rot is caught early by continuously exercising code.

check.a: Its dependencies, platforms and external services change around it.

anomalies-in-distributed-systems.core: Distributed systems add anomalies single machines don't have: partial failures, network partitions, clock skew, retries causing duplicates, and emergent cascades. The eight fallacies of distributed computing name the false assumptions.

first_principles.problem: Code that assumes the network is reliable, latency is zero and time is consistent works in testing and fails strangely in production.
derivation: Design for **partial failure**: timeouts, retries with idempotency.
Use **tracing** to follow requests across services.
Remember the **eight fallacies** (reliable network, zero latency, infinite bandwidth, secure network, stable topology, one admin, zero transport cost, homogeneous network).

analogy.title: Coordinating by post
analogy.story: Letters get lost, arrive out of order or twice, and each person's watch shows a different time.
analogy.breaks: Post delays are days; network delays are milliseconds but happen millions of times.

example.title: Double charges
example.scenario: A payment call times out and is retried.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: The server stores idempotency keys and returns the original result on retry.

check.q: Name three of the eight fallacies.
check.a: The network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite.
